site.name: Positive
site.intro: Five small retellings from India’s living story traditions. Read one, then return to your day a little lighter.

stories.title: Yasoda's Wonder in Gokula
body: In the cowherd village of Gokula, little Krishna was caught with earth on His lips, and when mother Yasoda playfully asked Him to open His mouth, she gasped at what she saw. Within that small mouth shone the entire universe — the sky, distant planets, oceans, mountains, and scattered stars.

Overwhelmed and trembling with love, Yasoda could only marvel at the vision filling her child's mouth, her heart swelling with a wonder too vast for words. The cosmic sight softened and faded, as though the magic itself could not bear to frighten her.

Dismissing it as the play of yogamaya, she gathered Krishna onto her lap once more, cradling Him close. Protected by his mother's boundless affection, the little one smiled and went on playing freely, the mystery settling gently into her heart.

stories.title: The Lake of Four Friends
body: Beside an ancient lake, four friends made their home beneath a great tree by the waterside. The mouse Hiranyaka, the crow Laghupatana, the tortoise Manthara, and the deer Dindima shared their food as one household and called out softly whenever danger drew near.

One day a fowler's snare caught one of the four, and the circle of loyalty held fast. Each in turn — quick wings, steady shell, gentle hooves — risked the path to bring the other home, until the lost one was safely returned to the lakeshore.

When the trouble passed, the four rested once more beneath the spreading branches, their friendship unbroken. So they spent the rest of their days in peace, warmed by the same old tree, fed by the same clear water, and watched over by the bond they had kept.

stories.title: Bharata Carries Rama's Sandals Home
body: When Bharata reached the quiet forests of Chitrakuta and found his elder brother Rama living as an exile, he begged him to return to Ayodhya. Rama, steadfast in his vow, gently refused and pressed his wooden paduka-sandals into his younger brother's hands.

He asked Bharata to place the padukas upon the throne and rule the kingdom as his humble representative. But Bharata, heart swelling with love and devotion, lifted the sacred sandals onto his own head and walked barefoot beside the royal chariot all the long way home.

In Ayodhya he governed wisely and justly for fourteen patient years, waiting faithfully by the throne for Rama's promised return, a quiet promise that kept the kingdom tenderly alive until its beloved lord came home at last.

stories.title: The Mouse-Maiden's Hidden Gift
body: During a long famine, a gentle mouse-maiden served her father in their humble home. Born of a celestial dancer through a curse of Brahma, she had a gift for telling truth wherever she went, and her quiet words brought comfort to those who listened.

When a poor brahmin despaired of feeding his family, the faithful mouse carried grain by night, hiding it deep in her hole. Each morning she brought it to the brahmin's door, day by day, until their small prosperity slowly returned and the household smiled again.
In time, the mouse-maiden took her rightful place in the grateful family. What began as a curse had become a quiet blessing, proving that steady kindness, even in famine, can turn sorrow into hope.

stories.title: Hanuman's Gift to Tulsidas
stories.source: Tulsidas hagiographic tradition (Bhaktamal and later hagiographies)
body: In Varanasi, the poet Tulsidas sat at the Hanuman temple, fasting and softly chanting Rama's name while scholars outside laughed at his humble origins. Night after night he kept his vigil, refusing to give up on his devotion.

Then Hanuman himself appeared in a vision, his presence radiant, and granted Tulsidas the gift of composing verses. He told the poet to write the Ramcharitmanas in the everyday language of the people, so every heart could hear Rama's story.

Tulsidas awoke with verses pouring from him like a river, and soon the Ramcharitmanas spread across North India, becoming a scripture of bhakti read in countless homes and turning mockery into lasting grace.
